### CHAPTER 55. Of Isaac's blessing of Jacob. Genesis 27. 395

29. We see very well in this figure <note>original: "figure"; here meaning a symbolic representation or type</note> that the blessing would *not rest* upon *Esau*, who by nature had a rugged, hairy beast's skin in his essence, although he was the first-born to whom the blessing belonged by right of inheritance. For the *first* man <note>Adam</note> had become depraved in his nature and had lost the inheritance of God; therefore, the blessing and the filial inheritance rest only upon the *second* new *Adam* <note>Christ</note>.

30. Furthermore, this figure denotes that the new man in Christ should take away the scepter and might from the *Devil*, and also from the *Man of Sin*. In this blessing, he should rule over him in power, just as *Jacob* was made Lord over his enemies. This figure points entirely to *Christ*.

31. For as *Jacob* took a strange form upon himself, coming in strange attire before his father to desire and obtain the blessing, so Christ—namely, the Eternal Word—also took on a strange form, which is our humanity, and brought that same humanity before his Father to be blessed.

32. And as <margin>Genesis 27:28</margin> *Isaac blessed his son Jacob with the dew of heaven and the fatness of the earth, with corn and wine*, even so God the Father blessed our humanity in Christ. For our humanity was also originally made from the *limus* <note>original: *limus*; Latin for mud or slime, referring to the "dust of the ground" used to create man</note> of the earth, and was nourished and brought up by the dew of heaven, even by corn and wine. God blessed this for the new birth and the *resurrection* of the dead into the life to come.

33. And as <margin>Genesis 27:29</margin> *Isaac appointed Jacob to be Lord over his brethren of the natural property*, so God has appointed the *new birth* in the blessing of Christ to be Lord over the Adamical <note>relating to the fallen nature of Adam</note> nature in flesh and blood. Thus, the new man, born of God's blessing, must rule over all the members of his natural body, and they must be subject to the new man.

34. And as <margin>Genesis 27:29</margin> *Isaac set the curse between them, saying that whoever should curse Jacob should be accursed, and whoever should bless him should also be blessed*, so God has set the curse upon the corrupt Adamical kingdom. Whoever is not found in the blessing of Christ must be eternally in the curse of God; but whoever brings his mind and will into this *Jacob's*—that is, *Christ's*—blessing, shall be in the blessing forever.

35. Furthermore, we see in this type <note>a symbolic person or event</note> how it goes with the children of God. For <margin>Genesis 27:30, 31, 32, 33</margin> *when Isaac had blessed Jacob, then Esau came with his venison, and his father Isaac was astonished and said, "Why? Who are you?"* He was dismayed that he had unknowingly blessed Jacob. This typifies how the Adamical man understands nothing at all of God's ways. It shows how God often wonderfully leads a person according to their inward spiritual ground. Although the person is carried along in the way of God, they still look much at outward reason and often stumble at external, rational things—at temporary orders and goods—and allow fear to seize them. Man would like the will of his own reason to be done, just as here Isaac *trembled* exceedingly when he saw that the will of his reason was broken.

36. And in this, we acknowledge the *misery* and ignorance of the children of God: that reason enters into its own dominion and will not wholly leave itself to God, and is astonished when things go differently than it had imagined for itself.

37. And then we see how God at last breaks forth with his light in the *understanding* and shows man his way, so that he is satisfied.

<summary>This page provides an allegorical interpretation of Isaac's blessing of Jacob, portraying Jacob as a figure for Christ (the "Second Adam") and the "new man" who must rule over the fallen "Adamical" nature. It explains that human reason often struggles to understand God's providential leading, which may contradict external expectations.</summary>

### **CHAPTER 55: Of Isaac's Blessing of Jacob (Genesis 27)**

...[Christ]ians <note>original: "frians"; likely a transcription error for "Christians"</note>, and desire the blessing of God, just as Esau stood and wept bitterly for the blessing. He did not mind the kingdom of God, but desired instead to be a lord upon the earth over his brothers and other men, and to possess riches and the "fullness of the belly" <note>original: "fullness of the Belly"; meaning physical satisfaction, wealth, or gluttony</note>.

44. This Esau, in his blessing, is a true type <note>a "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament that foreshadows something in the New Testament</note> of the ***Antichrist***. He draws near to God with his lips and gives himself to an external, superficial service and worship of Christ. He presents himself as if he does it for God, making grand, holy displays in his hypocrisy and "glittering verbalisms." He shows himself with zeal and devotion so that he might be honored by men, and so that his gods, **Mammon** <note>the personification of wealth</note> and **Maozim** <note>original: "Maozim," likely referring to the "god of fortresses" mentioned in Daniel 11:38, often interpreted as a false deity of power or worldly protection</note>, may be fat. He even mourns and laments out of malice when men will not do what he wants, or when he cannot get enough of the "belly-blessing" according to the will of his god **Maozim**. Whoever reproves or corrects him, or speaks to him of the true *Blessing* of God, he will seek to kill; he cannot endure a true servant of Christ beneath him.

45. Reason supposes that because *Isaac* said to *Esau*, "You shall live by your sword," God had commanded him to do so. Here, reason supports [its murdering malice and bloodthirsty villainy]. However, it is quite different: God does not will any war, but the kingdom of nature in God’s anger wills it. Whoever is born only of the kingdom of nature also lives according to it.

46. Therefore Isaac said, "You will do it," as if he should have said, "Through your anger you will serve the anger of God and will be a lord in the kingdom of nature in this world." This is just as the rich and wealthy bring themselves into power and authority, doing so through the kingdom of nature in wrath.

47. We see further how **Esau** hated his brother **Jacob** with a deadly hatred for the sake of the blessing <margin>Genesis 27:41</margin>. Nevertheless, Esau was not capable of receiving it within the kingdom of nature. This signifies that the true children of Christ shall be hated, persecuted, and killed by the children in the kingdom of nature for the sake of this blessing. This is because the kingdom of Grace shall rule over the kingdom of nature and destroy it at the end of days, transforming it into its own power <margin>Note when Grace shall rule</margin>. Therefore, there is strife between both kingdoms.

48. For the children of Christ in this lifetime live—as far as the "outward man" is concerned—in the kingdom of depraved human nature, that is, in the kingdom of the Esauites. Regarding the spirit, they are only strangers and pilgrims within it, as Christ said: "*My kingdom is not of this world*" <note>original: "Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo" (John 18:36)</note>. Therefore, the children of this world are enemies to them and persecute them, just as **Esau** persecuted his brother **Jacob**.

49. For where the kingdom of Christ begins to flourish, the kingdom of the Devil immediately begins to storm and rage. Because the kingdom of Christ will take away and ruin his power and princely throne, there is strife in this world between the children of **Jacob** and **Esau**.

50. As soon as **Jacob** had obtained the blessing, **Esau** intended in his mind to kill **Jacob** <margin>Genesis 27:41</margin>. This is a figure of Christ, showing how God’s anger would kill Him within this blessing in our assumed humanity (the kingdom of nature). It also shows that the children of God should also be...

# CHAPTER LVI.
## How Isaac and Rebecca sent Jacob away to another country because of Esau; and how the Lord appeared to him in a vision of a ladder that reached even into heaven; and how Esau behaved himself afterward toward his parents.
### Based on the 28th Chapter of Genesis.

<margin>Genesis 28</margin> 1. When Jacob had received the blessing, he had to depart from his native home and from his father and mother, and flee from the wrath of Esau. This is now a representation <note>original: "figure"</note> of Christ, showing how He—after He had assumed and anointed our humanity—should flee with our humanity out of its Adamic <note>Relating to the fallen, earthly state of Adam.</note> father's house and back into the original house of Paradise.

2. It further signifies that the children of Christ (after they have received the anointing <note>original: "Unction"</note> and blessing, and the new birth begins to spring forth in them through that blessing) shall and must immediately flee with their thoughts and minds from their father Adam's house of depraved nature. It shows that the Devil and the world soon hate them, and they must immediately commit themselves to the path of Christ's pilgrimage. They must live under the world's slave-like yoke, in misery and oppression, in disfavor and disrespect. For God leads them forth, with their thoughts and minds, out of their father's house—namely, <note>original: "viz."</note> out of the desire for flesh and blood—so that they do not care at all for the pleasures of the world and flee from it, just as Jacob fled from his father's house.

3. And then we see how wonderfully God guides his children and defends them from their enemies, so that the Devil, acting in God's anger, cannot kill them unless it is God's will. Just as He defended Jacob from the fury of Esau and led him away from him, we have here an excellent example in Jacob. He forsook his native home, and also his father and mother, for the sake of this blessing; he loved God more than all worldly <note>original: "temporall"</note> goods and willingly left everything to Esau, so that he might simply be the one blessed by God.

4. And we see that when he had left the riches of the world in his father's house, the Lord appeared to him with eternal goods. <margin>Genesis 28:12</margin> He showed him a ladder upon which he could ascend into God's eternal Kingdom. This ladder was none other than Christ, whom he had "put on" through the lineage of the Covenant. Here, the symbolic representation <note>original: "type"</note> was shown to him, revealing what kind of Person Christ should be.

<margin>Genesis 28:12</margin> 5. For this ladder (as he perceived it) was upon the earth, and its top reached into heaven; and the angels of God ascended and descended upon it. This signifies that God's eternal Word, with the power of heaven—namely, with the essence of the angelic divine world—should descend...

Jacob's ladder is identified as a symbolic "type" of Christ, acting as the bridge between the earthly and divine realms.</summary>

### CHAPTER 56. Of Jacob's Ladder. Genesis 28. Page 399

5. ...or immerse itself into our essence (which had departed from God and was blind toward God) and assume our humanity. In this way, He united heaven with the world in man, so that humanity, through this entrance of the Deity into humanity, might have a ladder to God.

6. It shows that mankind should come through Christ’s humanity into the society of the angels (Matthew 12:22). This is clearly signified here by the angels of God ascending and descending on this ladder. It also shows that heaven should be opened again in man through this entrance of the divine essence into humanity, and that the children of God should have the angels as companions in this world—which God showed to Jacob by the angels coming up and down to him on this ladder.

7. This shall be a very great comfort to the children of God who turn themselves from their father’s house—that is, from *this world’s vanity*—to this Jacob's Ladder. For they shall certainly know that God’s angels come to them upon this ladder to which they have turned themselves, and are willingly around them to serve them.

8. For this ladder properly signifies the pilgrim’s path of Christ through this world into God’s kingdom. The kingdom of the corrupt Adamic <note>original: "Adamicall" — referring to the fallen nature inherited from Adam</note> nature always still clings to the children of God and *hinders* them in flesh and blood in the spirit of this world. Therefore, according to the inward man in Christ’s spirit, they must continually ascend through many crosses and tribulations on this ladder, following Christ under His cross and red banner <note>The "Red Banner" is a traditional symbol for the blood of Christ and the victory won through suffering.</note>.

9. On the contrary, the world lives in the pleasure of their father Adam’s house, in scorn, jeering, and mocking, in envy, spite, and malice. Whatever they can do to cross and vex these children of Jacob, they joy and take delight in, laughing and sneering at them. We have an example of this in Esau: out of contempt, disdain, and spite toward his father and mother, he took *Ishmaelite wives*, who were of the line of mockery or reviling. These were pure bitterness of spirit and grief of heart to both Isaac and Rebecca.

10. Here we clearly see that the Devil has *his power* in the kingdom of this world in the corrupt human property. He continually resists God’s children, *vexes* and plagues them, and fights with them for his kingdom, which he has lost and does not willingly grant <note>original: "beteem" — to permit or allow someone to have something</note> to them.

11. And we see very clearly how the *Lord* stands above on this ladder of the pilgrimage of Christ, as He did with Jacob. Without ceasing, He calls the children of Christ and comforts them, so that they should cheerfully ascend upon it. He will not leave them but will come to them and bless them, so that their **seed** and fruit shall grow, increase, and <margin>Genesis 28:14</margin> be **as the dust upon the earth**. This means that in their toil, labor, and anxiety, they shall spring up and flourish in the inward divine kingdom.

12. For as much as the children of Christ go out from this world and forsake it in their mind, so much do they spring up in the inward kingdom of Christ. There, God stands above upon this ladder and continually *inspires* or *inspeaks* <note>original: "inſpeaketh" — Boehme's term for the process of God speaking His living Word into the human soul</note> His blessing and power into them, <margin>John 15:5</margin> so that they grow as **branches on His vine**, <margin>Psalm 80:15</margin> which He has planted again in...

It contrasts the spiritual struggles of "Jacob's children" with the worldly malice of those following the "Adamic" nature.</summary>

13. And we clearly see by this that this whole type <note>a "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament believed to foreshadow something in the New Testament</note>, from Abraham to Jacob, contains mere figures of the kingdom and person of Christ and his children. For here God renews the promised covenant of Abraham concerning the "seed of the woman" with Jacob also: that out of his seed, as out of the line of the covenant, He should come who should bless all nations. For this cause Jacob was also led from his father’s house; God having set before him outwardly the kingdom of Christ in this figure. For Christ's sake, God caused his wrath to cease from the children of unbelief and did not destroy them, but gave them time to repent, and so appeased his wrath in this type, which pointed at the fulfillment which was to come.

14. We have here also a firm ground and assurance that Christ has truly taken upon himself our Adam-like <note>original: Adamical</note> soul and humanity in the body of Mary, and has destroyed Death, Hell, and the anger of God in our humanity which he assumed, and has set up this ladder of Jacob. For God said to Jacob: <margin>Genesis 28:14</margin> *Through you and your seed shall all the generations of the earth be blessed;* through you, Jacob, through your own seed, which is God and Man—namely <note>original: viz.</note>, the heavenly divine essence <term>Ens: a Latin term for being or substance</term> and substance, and the human essence and substance, in the power of the eternal Word.

15. In which Word, the holy name Jesus—namely, the highest love of the Deity—has unfolded and manifested itself in our humanity which he has assumed. This love of God alone <note>original: sola Love</note> in the name of Jesus has overcome the wrath of the eternal nature in our souls (which comes from the Father's property in anger) and has changed it into the love of divine joy. It has broken the silent death which had severed us from the life of God and has manifested the divine life of the highest holy life-force <term>Tincture: a term in mystical chemistry/theology for the spiritual essence or life-giving power of God</term> in the eternal speaking Word of the divine power, in death, and has made death to be life. And so our soul, in this divine power, is simultaneously penetrated and pressed through death and the anger of God.

16. And it is in no way to be understood as some say: that the substance in which the Word became man did not proceed from Adam. Some erroneously say that the Virgin Mary did not descend from mankind, and that she only outwardly took upon her a human body from Anna and is not from the seed of Joachim, but is an eternal virgin chosen by God for this purpose before the world was.

17. This text teaches us otherwise, where God says, *Through you and your seed*—not through a strange divine seed only, but through you and your seed. With the entrance of the divine substance, Christ should break death in Adam's soul and body, and destroy hell in Adam's soul and body, which was manifested or revealed in Paradise.

18. For here lay our sickness and misery, which Christ took upon himself as a yoke. Christ sacrificed his Father's wrath, which was kindled in our humanity, and awakened his highest love in our human and his holy blood. His holy essence <note>original: Tincture</note> entered into our human death and infused <note>original: tinctured</note> our (in Adam) faded heavenly substantiality—which faded in Adam when he brought worldliness and the false will into it—and raised up our faded heavenly substance with his heavenly living...

20. They were indeed united in the Incarnation, or the becoming human, so that they are inseparable. In this way, the masculine and feminine properties might be entirely changed back into one image again, as Adam was before his Eve, when he was neither man nor woman but a masculine virgin. <note>The author refers to a common mystical belief that the original Adam was an androgynous being before the creation of Eve.</note>

21. Therefore, Christ took his soul from a woman—namely from a virgin—and yet was a man, so that he stood rightly in the Adamic image. He brought the averted, severed properties of life (in which our will had broken itself off from God) back into <term>balance</term> <note>original: "Temperature"; meaning a state of perfect harmony or proper proportion</note> and union, namely into that ONE.

22. For Adam turned his will away from the only will of God, and Jesus Christ took our soul back into the only will of God; he turned the will of our soul—in our humanity, which he assumed—into the only will of God again.

23. But so that the reader may be thoroughly and fundamentally informed about what our soul is and what the Word that became human is, compare the two: our soul, before the beginning of the <margin>Of the soul.</margin> human creaturely soul, was an essence of the Word of God within the Word (John 1). And yet, it was inspired or spoken from the speaking Word of God into the human image in a natural and creaturely life, and formed into an image of the Eternal speaking Word. This creaturely life of the soul turned itself in Adam away from the divine speaking and into its own will and speaking; in this respect, it was broken off from the most unsearchable substance and separated from God.

24. Into this separated word—namely, into the soul—the only Eternal divine speaking Word gave itself again. It turned the will of the soul back into the Eternal One, namely into God's Eternal speaking. Therefore, the soul is indeed from the Eternal Word. But Christ—namely the highest love of the Deity—did not take a new soul out of the Eternal speaking. Instead, he took our soul—namely the Word which was once spoken or formed in Adam, our human soul—into his love-speaking through the grace and union of the Deity.

25. Immediately after the Fall in Paradise, God spoke into our poor fallen soul again, establishing the covenant and the root of his highest love and grace through the Word, as a center of grace for conception and for the new regeneration.

27. This Word, in its spiritual figure in the Virgin Mary, was at the limit—namely <note>original: "viz."</note>, at the end of the spiritual form—where that same spiritual form of the Word of God was contained in a substantial being <term>original: "Ens"; a philosophical term for essence or existence</term>. 28. This contained spiritual image, which was the seed of faith that Abraham laid hold of in faith, was bestowed upon Isaac, and from Isaac upon Jacob <margin>Genesis 28:14</margin>. And to Jacob, God said, "Through you and your seed shall all the people of the Earth be blessed"; namely, through this seed of faith which Jacob had received from his father Isaac in this line of the Covenant. This line of faith had incorporated itself into the human property, according to the inward ground of the second principle—that is, in that image of the heavenly world's substance which was extinguished in Adam.
29. In this incorporated ground, the limit of God's Covenant remained in a spiritual form until Mary. It was passed from person to person, from Adam and Eve all the way to Mary. There, the Word of Divine Power was moved and essentially assumed our human flesh and blood together with the soul. It made alive the extinguished heavenly being <term>Ens</term> in the seed of Mary on our behalf. This manifestation penetrated and also pressed into Mary’s heavenly substantiality, so that she became living in regard to that heavenly virginity which disappeared in Eve. In this living virginity—that is, in Adam’s heavenly matrix <note>The "matrix" refers to the womb or the fundamental creative source of life</note>—God became man.
30. And this is the blessing of Mary above all other women <margin>Luke 1:42</margin>: that she is the first since Adam in whom the heavenly matrix became opened, and in which the dry rod of Aaron rightly budded <note>A reference to Numbers 17:8, symbolizing a miraculous life springing from what was dead</note>—namely, the kingdom of God. She is the first in whom the hidden power was manifested, for in her, the limit of the Covenant in the spiritual image or type was at an end, and in her, it was fulfilled with <margin>In or by.</margin> our humanity.
31. Nevertheless, she is truly the daughter of Adam, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, both in regard to her humanity and the Covenant of the spiritual figure. In her conception, when the inward incorporated image or type of the inspired <note>literally "in-spoken"</note> Covenant of Grace (which was laid hold of in faith) assumed our human property, then was the kingdom of Christ manifested in the flesh <margin>1 Timothy 3:16</margin>.
32. In this kingdom, the faithful afterward "put on" Christ in the flesh through their faith, yet only in regard to that heavenly image extinguished in Adam (just as Mary did). There, Christ embraces the poor soul in His arms and encompasses them with the power of God. He infuses and flows into them with His love, which preserves and defends them from the wrath of God, from sin, death, the devil, and hell.
33. This is a brief summary of the true foundation of what the Spirit of God prefigured and represented through the Patriarchs. He led them so wonderfully and alluded to the figure of Christ to show how it would come to pass afterward.

36. For where God withdraws himself from a person, sin and the anger of God will always be first manifested in that person, so that he will acknowledge and tremble at his sin and enter into repentance. Then God’s friendly countenance appears to him and comforts him; for if the soul goes out from sin, then God’s Grace enters into it. Then the soul says, *surely the Lord was with me in my anxiety, and I did not know it; now I see that the Lord is with the troubled heart,* which is troubled in a divine zeal; *there is the place of God and the gate of Heaven.*

37. Furthermore, it signifies how the highest love of God in this Covenant in Christ would be immersed into our humanity, and how the humanity of Christ would be occupied with trouble, in that he took upon himself all our trouble and misery. This is as it was here for Jacob, when in his trouble he had to depart from his father’s house in fear and trembling because of his brother Esau, who lay in wait to murder him. All of this is a figure concerning Christ: when God’s anger in our humanity lay in wait to murder him, he would be in an agony, heaviness, and distress, and he would pray to his Father, and his Father would comfort him. All of this was done before <margin>Or, his Passion.</margin> he was crucified, especially in the *Mount of Olives*, in which place this figure of Jacob was fulfilled.

38. And as <margin>Genesis 28:18</margin> Jacob took the stone which he had laid under his head and *set it up for a remembrance, and poured oil upon it;* so has Christ set up his anguish or agony for a remembrance to us poor men, and poured forth his oil of joy and victory upon it in our troubled, terrified hearts. And from that same <margin>Agony, and a troubled heart, because of sin.</margin> stone, he has erected his Church for a continual remembrance; of all which this type of Jacob was a prefiguration.

39. Jacob signifies this in plain words where he says: <margin>Genesis 28:20, 21, 22</margin> *If God will be with me and defend me in the way which I travel, and give me bread to eat and clothes to put on, and bring me home in peace to my father, then shall the Lord be my God, and this stone, which I have set up for a pillar, shall be God’s house, and of all which you give to me, I will give the tenth to you.* Where, under this figure, he clearly signifies the Levitical and afterwards the Evangelical priesthood, as it would be hereafter.

# CHAPTER LVIII.

### How Jacob served his <margin>stepfather</margin> <note>original: "Father in Law"</note> twenty years, and fathered twelve sons and one daughter, and how God blessed him so that he obtained great wealth, and how Laban often changed his wages and yet could not hurt him; what is to be understood by this.

->**Based on the 30th Chapter of Genesis.**<-

1. We see in this history especially how it goes with the children of God in this world: how they must live in nothing but trials <note>original: "meere Crosses"</note> and adversity, as Jacob did with his wives. For <margin>Genesis 30:1</margin> when Rachel saw that she was barren, she envied her sister Leah, to signify that man's own love seeks not the honor of God but itself. Just as Rachel now envied Leah because she had a reputation for being blessed by God, and said to Jacob, "Give me children also, if not, I die."

2. Here we see how the ways of God are quite hidden to reason, although reason stands within the symbolism of divine wonders. This is represented here by Rachel, who signifies the own <term>Adamic nature</term> <note>Referring to the fallen, natural state of humanity inherited from Adam.</note> which desires the power of life from the blessing of God; and if it does not get the same, it must die. Indeed, the "spirit of zeal" in her desire very well signifies her inner <term>Ground</term> <note>In the mystical theology of the author, "Ground" (Ungrund/Grund) refers to the underlying spiritual essence or source of being.</note> in the Covenant of God. But her reason did not understand it; she only desired children so that she might be delivered from disgrace. But her inner Ground stood hidden and panted through the human nature to manifest itself in the human essence. Therefore, the inner Ground in the Covenant of Grace signifies—through its own Adamic essence—that if the inner ground should not be manifested through the human essence, it must then die eternally. Therefore reason says, "Give me children or else I die," which outwardly seems to be an opposition and discouragement. But the Spirit of God has its symbol here, under which it has its meaning.

3. And then we see in both these sisters, who were yet daughters of God’s Covenant in the Promise, how the poison of the serpent in the wrath of God in flesh and blood so vehemently sets itself against the line of Christ in the Covenant and always despises the same. **CH. 59. *How Jacob departed from Laban. Genesis 31.*** **419**

Regarding this departure to his Father: the Devil and the wicked world would scorn him and completely slay him. They would take away and rob him of his goods, as well as of the children he had fathered. This is exactly what the Devil did through the Pharisees and wicked Jews, who wanted to take away and rob Christ of all his faithful children—just as Laban pursued and hunted after Jacob, wanting to take his purchased goods away from him again.

8. But just as God would not allow Laban to hurt Jacob, so God would not <margin>Gen. 31:7</margin> allow the Devil and the wicked high priests to rob Christ of his purchased goods. Although they slew his outward humanity, he rose again from the dead and brought his purchased goods into his Father’s country.

9. In this chapter, the Spirit of Moses represents a **wonderful figure** <note>original: "figure", meaning a symbolic type or prophetic foreshadowing</note> which ought to be carefully observed because he hints at a secret mystery within it. For he says: <margin>Gen. 31:19, 20, 30, 33, 34</margin> *When Jacob fled from Laban, Rachel had stolen her father's idols.* He further says: *Thus Jacob stole away the heart of Laban the Syrian <note>original: "stole away the heart", a Hebrew idiom meaning he deceived or outwitted him</note> in that he did not tell him that he fled.* We see further how Laban, when he caught up to Jacob, was eager to find his idols and searched all of Jacob’s household goods for them. We also see in this text how Rachel was the one who loved those idols; she sat upon them and hid them so that her father could not get them back.

10. In these words, an **outward** and an **inward** figure is represented to us, showing how it would go with Israel in the future. These idols were *not* heathenish idols associated with the constellation or star *Molech* <margin>Acts 7:43</margin>—as the heathens had—but as we read, they made images, monuments, statues, or pictures of their deceased friends as a pattern for instruction. Among the heathens, these images were later turned into idols. These may well have been such images of his dead kindred, which Laban was loath to lose because they were patterns of instruction and memorials to him of his ancestors and deceased relatives whom he loved.

11. But the true figure at which the Spirit points regarding the future is this: First, that Israel would *not* continually cling to God with their whole heart. Instead, they would always take these idols of fleshly self-love along with them. They would love themselves and their own "images"—namely, genealogies of human greatness, status, high birth, and noble pedigrees of **gentility** <note>original: "Gentility", referring here to noble social rank or aristocratic lineage</note>—more than God, just as it eventually happened.

12. Specifically, Jacob's departure hints at the departure of Israel out of Egypt into the Promised Land. At that time, they also took their fleshly idols with them and soon after <margin>1 Sam. 8:8</margin> served their own idols—namely, human greatness. They forsook their God and respected their **Mammon** <note>original: "Mammon", a term for wealth or property, often personified as a false god</note>. They insisted on having <margin>1 Sam. 8:19</margin> kings among them according to the custom of the **heathen** <note>original: "Heathen", meaning non-Christian or pagan nations</note> and forsook their rightful King, who had brought them out of Egypt.

13. Secondly, it suggests how Christ—whom Jacob represented—would take to himself this "Rachel" in our flesh and blood. This represents the soul’s "idol-wills" (inherited from Adam) which have turned away from God. The soul has acquired these images and idols for itself and possessed them as Rachel did. Christ would bring these diverted wills of the soul, along with their acquired idols and images, out of the "idol's house" or temple. These idols are the idol-wills and desires...

How Esau went to meet Jacob with four hundred men, soldiers, what this signifies; and how Jacob sent a present to his brother Esau, and how a man wrestled with him the whole night. What all this means. Genesis 32.

->For the reader’s deep consideration.<-

5. ...servants, and camels, with other cattle, so that he might with all this find grace and favor with his lord Esau. So also Christ says to his Father, in our humanity (that is, in Adam) which he has assumed: he has been long abroad, absent from the kingdom of God, and has <margin>Born, generated, or begotten</margin> brought forth many images out of the divine wisdom through the formation of nature in the kingdom of this world in God’s works of wonder. He did this so that he might, with these formations of wonders, find grace and favor with God—seeing these wonders were brought forth through the nature of his manifested wrath—so that they might come to the eternal divine vision and contemplation.

6. But the anger went to meet him in the <margin>the four elements</margin> four elements and would devour their earthliness and evil. For Esau’s four hundred men signify nothing else but the wrath of nature in the four elements of the body, and they went to meet the humanity of Christ. When Christ was bringing the created image of Adam in our humanity into God (that is, into Paradise), then the wrath of God first wanted to kill the Adamic image so that it might no longer live in the kingdom of anger, seeing as it was meant to live in God.

7. <margin>Genesis 32:9, 10, 11</margin> And as Jacob humbled himself before God and said, "O God of my father Abraham and God of my father Isaac, Lord, you who have said to me, 'Return again into your country and to your kindred, and I will deal well with you'; I am unworthy of the least of all your mercy, and all your faithfulness and truth which you have afforded to your servant. For I had nothing but this staff with which I went over this Jordan, and now I have become two bands. Deliver me from the hand of my brother, from the hand of Esau, for I am afraid of him, lest he come and strike me, along with the mothers and the children." So also Christ humbles himself in our assumed humanity before God. And though God, speaking through the prophet David regarding our assumed humanity, <margin>Psalm 110:1</margin> has bidden him to sit at his right hand until he has laid all his enemies under his footstool, yet he humbles himself. Even as Jacob did before the anger of Esau, so also did Christ before the anger of his Father.

8. And as Jacob said, "When I went over this Jordan I had only this staff, but now I have become two bands," so also when Christ—that is, the eternal Word of Divine Love—came to us in our humanity, then it was only the staff of divine grace. But in our humanity in the servant's house of Adam, he was enriched with two bands: namely, a twofold humanity—the heavenly nature that was extinguished in Adam, and the earthly nature from the <term>limus</term><note>original: "Limus" (Latin for slime or mud), referring to the "dust of the ground" from which Adam was created.</note> of the earth. Therefore he says in this twofold humanity, as Jacob said to God, "O God of my father Abraham, and God of my father Isaac, O Lord, you have said to me, 'Return again into your country and to your first kindred'; I am less than the least of all these mercies which you have bestowed on your servant." This signifies that it was only through divine mercy that these two bands (the twofold humanity) returned home again into their first country of Paradise to their angelic kindred.

9. And when Jacob had humbled himself before God and his brother Esau, <margin>Genesis 32:13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18</margin> he stayed there all night and took from what he had on hand a present for his brother Esau: two hundred female goats and twenty male goats, two hundred ewes and twenty rams, thirty milch <note>modern: nursing or milk-giving</note> camels with their colts, forty cows and ten bulls, and twenty female donkeys with ten colts. He put them under the care of his servants, every herd by itself, and said to them:

22. For the Covenant of Grace in love and the soul stood together in one person. Therefore, at that time, the soul of Jacob—acting as a figure and type of Christ—had to wrestle with God’s righteousness concerning the heavenly <term>Ens</term> <note>original: "Ens"; a philosophical term meaning "essence" or "inner being"</note>. This concerns the substantial Wisdom which the name Jesus brought along with the poor soul in its heavenly substance <note>The author uses "substantiality" to mean a spiritual reality or "body" that was lost by Adam</note>, which had faded in Adam. Through this, Adam’s faded substance sprang forth again in this living reality as a new birth.

23. Therefore, the Spirit of God says to Jacob: "You have wrestled with God and man"—namely, with God’s love in the covenant and with the future heavenly substance. This substance became man in the seed of Mary, and you have prevailed. For Christ, whom Jacob represented, was to wrestle with God’s righteousness in our assumed humanity and conquer.

24. And the Spirit in Moses says here: *And when he saw that he did not prevail against him* (meaning God’s righteousness in the anger of judgment did not prevail against grace), *then he touched the hollow of his thigh, and the hollow of his thigh was displaced as he wrestled with him.*

25. This signifies the destruction and displacing of the Adamic humanity. When Christ achieved this victory, then human self-power and self-will were displaced, broken, and killed. But just as Jacob did not die from this wrestling, even though his hip was indeed displaced, our humanity shall not die eternally, but only be displaced—that is, be changed.

26. This signifies especially how the repentant person must enter into this combat of Jacob and wrestle with God and man in the Spirit of Christ against God’s righteousness in the anger. When he overcomes, the "thigh" of his fleshly self-will will be broken. He must then go about in this world as one who is half-lame, unable to walk properly in the ways of the world. He goes "halting," as if his limbs were half-broken, leaving behind the playfulness and vanity of this world. For the Spirit, in Christ's victory, touches his thigh so that he is half-lame toward the pride and malice of this world and never cares for it again. Instead, he goes about as a despised, lame man. Those in the pride of the world, in their healthy <note>original: "haile"</note> and frolicsome jollity, pay him little regard; they consider him a lame, halting man who cannot follow the fashion <note>original: "Garb"</note> of the foolish <note>original: "Antick"</note> tricks, conceited jokes, and lustfulness of this world. But he has wrestled with God and man, and he is touched and marked by this victory.

27. The pride and playfulness of this world do not understand this. They still go about in God’s severe righteousness, in the kingdom of nature, in the power of fire, and in self-will. They think they are doing very well until the judgment takes its place; then the poor...

28. And as **Jacob** stood in the wrestling and had his thigh touched so that he limped <note>original: "halted"</note>, then the man said to him: *“Let me go, for the daybreak dawns.”* But he answered, *“I will not let you go except you bless me.”*

29. This is first the figure of Christ, when he yielded himself up in the righteousness of God in the Father’s anger, so that the anger slew him according to our humanity. Then the righteousness said: “Now let me go, for at present the **Eternal Morning breaks forth in me.**” But Christ had taken hold of the righteousness and said: “I will not let you go except you bless **humanity again**, so that the judgment may cease; except you bring the morning of your inward power forth through humanity, so that the curse may cease and that man may wholly stand in the divine working again, in the **Blessing.**”

30. Secondly, it is the beautiful <note>original: "faire"</note> type or image showing how it goes with the repentant man when he gives himself up through earnest repentance into this **Combat of Christ.** In Christ’s suffering and death, in his victory, and in the **spirit of Christ**, he wrestles with God’s severe righteousness, which continually assaults him in his **conscience.**

31. For God’s righteousness in the conscience says: *“Let me go; you are dead in sin and have no part in the divine grace. You have purposely and willfully sinned and set grace behind your back. Now you are mine; praying will not help you. I will not let you attain grace in your conscience; you will obtain **no more comfort** from God. The morning will no longer rise for you in your conscience, for you are a child of death. Now leave off and let me alone, so that I may shut you up below in the **dungeon** or chamber of death.”*

32. When this happens, then the poor soul wholly immerses itself into the **death of Christ** and gives itself up to the severe righteousness of God into the judgment, for the judgment lays hold of it. But the soul catches hold of the incorporated grace in the death of Christ and dives with it into the most inward ground of the judgment of God. In that ground, God’s love has **broken forth through the righteousness** and through the **judgment** (that is <note>original: "viz."</note>, through the eternal night) and has made that same night in man to be day.

33. Into this day—namely, into the **Abyss** without any human possibility or ability—the soul dives like a **child** that neither can nor will do anything more. It feels too unworthy of all grace and must indeed give itself up to the judgment. But with **this diving**, the soul yields <note>original typo: "yeedeth"</note> all its utmost will and ability and is in itself as it were void of nature and creature. It falls again into the **Word** in which it stood in the eternal speaking before its creaturely <note>creaturely: relating to the status of a created being</note> nature existed.

34. For God’s righteousness and judgment have no deeper ground than merely the **creaturely life.** But when the will of the soul yields itself up in going forth from the creature and sinks into the Abyss, then it is again **like a new child.** For the Abyss in the eternal speaking Word—out of which the highest love and grace of God has manifested itself—lays hold of it and penetrates into it, just as the sun does into the <term>Ens</term> <note>original: "Ens"; an alchemical and philosophical term for the "essence" or "being" of a thing</note> of a herb, from which the herb becomes half-solar, or of the nature of the sun. Thus in this **diving**, the soul in its will is **half-divine**, and

40. When the *Sun* of grace with its working power arises in the soul, then the soul rejoices and would always gladly behold the countenance of God in a creaturely <note>original: "creaturely manner"; referring to the way a created being perceives things</note> manner; as also *Moses* desired. The soul always thinks God is of some form; they do not yet look rightly upon God, but want to know God through *imagery*. Thus, creaturely *imagery* lies heavily upon us in the fallen, rebellious self-will of the mind, so that we cannot at all understand what God is—namely, that he himself is the abyss <note>original: "abysse"; the bottomless depth or origin of all things</note> of all nature and every creature—namely, the eternal ONE that dwells in nothing but only in himself, and has no form, nor anything else.

41. And it would be very well and good if we were not so led by the "Masters of the Letter" <note>those who interpret scripture only literally without spiritual insight</note> into an *imaginary* form when they teach and speak of the only God, as has been done until now. Men have led us into empty *images* <margin>Or, in.</margin> of the essential will, as if the only God willed this or that; whereas he himself is the sole will for the existence of nature and every creature. The whole creation lies only and alone in the *formation* of his expressed word and will, and the separation of the only will in that *expression*; and it is understood in its impression <margin>of.</margin> upon nature.

42. If the pride of *Lucifer* might be torn out of the hearts and eyes of these *Masters*, then men would soon see the countenance of God. But the "Babylonish Tower" <note>referring to the Tower of Babel; symbolic of human pride and religious confusion</note> upon which men try to climb—climbing up to God in *opinions* into a *separated heaven* where God sits cooped up—this withholds true knowledge and understanding. It makes us always ask: What is the name of God? Where is God? What is the will of God? Also, they say God wills good and evil, from which they make a multitude of <margin>Or, determinations and conclusions.</margin> decrees in the divine purpose, just as a *prince* in his land makes laws. They have as much understanding of God and his will as a *pot* understands of the *potter*.

43. It is to be lamented that we are so blindly led, and the *truth* withheld, in *imaginary concepts* <margin>imaginary concepts.</margin>. For if the divine power in the inward ground <note>the fundamental essence or center of the soul</note> of the soul were manifest and working with its brilliance, and if men did *desire* to go forth from their ungodly ways and give themselves up to God, then the whole Triune God would be *present* in the life and will of the soul. The heaven wherein God dwells would be opened in the soul; and there, in the soul, is the *place* of God, where the Father begets his Son, and where the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

44. For God makes use of no restricted place. He dwells even in the *abyss* of the wicked soul, but he is incomprehensible to it as far as his love is concerned; but as to his anger, he is *manifest* and comprehensible in the wicked soul.

45. For the eternal <margin>Or, expression.</margin> speaking of the Word, which is incomprehensible to nature and creature, becomes <margin>conceivable, or perceptible, or takes on an idea.</margin> imaged in the will of the soul; of which the Scripture says: <margin>Psalm 18:25, 26.</margin> *With the holy you are holy, and with the perverse you are perverse.* Also, such as the people are, such a God they have.

46. For in the thrones of the holy angels, God is manifest in his *love*, and in the thrones of the devils he is manifest in his *wrath*—namely, according to darkness and torment. And yet there is but one only God, and *not* two; according to the tormenting nature he wills...

50. For God’s Spirit did not perform such wonders just for the sake of the history of a plain, simple shepherd, as it appears in its outward form. Nor did He express those things so exactly in writing because He was so concerned with history that He preserved it among all people and allowed it to be proclaimed as His word. No, certainly not; it was for this reason: that under such plain, simple historical stories, something else is signified. With these, God’s Spirit alludes to what is future and eternal in a symbolic way. Therefore, men should look upon the Scriptures of the Old Testament with clearer eyes, for the whole New Testament is hidden within it in the symbolic form of plain, simple acts <margin>Apostolic history <note>original: "Apostel Geschichte"</note>. 432 **Gen. 33. How Jacob and Esau met. CHAP. 6.**

[The Son of God was to] become Man, so that God’s seed should overcome the corrupted seed of Adam with great divine Love, and quench the Father’s Anger with Love. This Love should wholly give itself into the Anger of the soul, so that God’s *Grace, Compassion*, and *Mercy* in that Love may pass through the Anger and also *change* the Anger into Compassion. As it is shown here, *Jacob*, with his present and great submission and humility, yielded himself to his brother *Esau*. He changed the Anger which Esau bore toward *Jacob* (regarding the natural right of the first-born and the Blessing) into such great *Compassion* that *Esau* fell upon his neck and wept in great compassion, and the anger in him was turned into Love. In the same way, Christ—with his great love and humility in our assumed <margin>\* The angry soul.</margin> humanity in our fiery, burning, angry soul—changed his Father’s Anger into such great *Mercy* and Compassion that the divine righteousness in that *Anger* ceased and departed from our souls.

3. For as *Jacob* appeased his brother *Esau* with the gift and humility when he gave himself up to the Anger of *Esau*, so also Christ appeased the Anger of God when he gave up his heavenly Blood with the great Tincture <note>original: "Tincture"; in Böhme’s writing, this refers to a spiritual force or medicinal essence that can transform or "color" a substance—here, the power of Love to transform Anger.</note> of Love into the Anger of God to be devoured. Then the Anger—namely, the nature of the dark world which was manifested in *Adam*—was *turned again* into the divine Light of Love; that is, into a Love-fire.

45. The creature is a dense, solidified vapor and *exhalation* from the *Word* <note>original: "word"; referring to the Divine Word or Logos through which all things were made</note>. Just as the Word is exhaled out of the free *will*, where the free will brings itself out of the abyss into depth, so also the free will of the angels and souls brings the *Word* into a depth. That depth is the creature—*namely*, a fiery source for its own "re-speaking." From that re-speaking proceed *evil* and *good*, and according to that re-spoken substance and power, the soul receives its judgment and sentence.

46. For *Judgment* is the separation of evil from the *good*, so that everything may possess its own principle. Whatever soul now speaks forth a *hellish* source—*namely*, the curse—it must enter into *death*, so that it no longer brings God’s Word into both evil and good, but into evil alone, so that everything may remain with its own kind.

47. Because in this world, through the *Word*, evil and good are spoken forth, *therefore* a final day of separation is appointed for this place. At that time, good and evil shall cease to be spoken together in any one place. The wicked shall have *their prepared place* where evil shall be spoken throughout eternity, so that the good may be known and, in the good, joy may be made manifest. Also, this is so that it may be known what *evil* and *good* are, as well as what life and death are, so that the children of God may *rejoice*.

48. For if evil were not known, joy would not be manifest. But if joy is manifest, then the eternal Word is spoken in joy—which is the reason the *Word*, along with *nature*, brought itself into a Creation.

49. This is the true foundation upon which all conceits and *opinions* are recognized, and all *sophistry* <note>original: "sophistry"; clever but false arguments intended to deceive</note> is thrown to the ground; here, all strife and contention ends. Whoever truly sees and understands this has no further *questions* about anything, for he sees that he lives and exists in God. He surrenders himself to God, so that he may further know and will through Him, and speak what and how He wills. Such a person seeks only the state of *lowliness* <note>original: "lowliness"; humility</note>, so that God alone may be exalted within him.

50. But as long as Lucifer <note>The author uses Lucifer to represent the spiritual principle of pride and self-will.</note> has his dominion in man, the creature presses forward to promote itself and wants to be its *own God*. That is also a wonder: just as God’s wisdom stands among the wonders in Love, it is also present in the "self" and in the creature's desire for its own possession.

51. Everything is good within its own principle where it lives, but it is opposite to another principle. Yet it must be this way so that one may be *manifested* in the other, and the hidden wisdom may be known. It is like a "sport" or game played out in the separation, through which the depth—*namely*, the Eternal One—may play with itself, before itself.

52. We should therefore learn to understand the *Scriptures* correctly regarding how God wills good and evil. Namely, the determination is not within His *very self*, but in His expressed Word—*that is*, in nature and the *creature*. God hated *Esau* in his corrupt nature, in *Esau’s* own self-nature; *Esau* was the archetype <note>original: "type"; a symbolic representation or foreshadowing</note> of hatred itself. But in God’s self—*namely*, in the imprinted or inspired Covenant of *Grace*—He loves him.

53. Therefore, He presents the archetype of Christ—*namely*, his brother *Jacob*—alongside him, and lets them *both* come from *one* seed. This signifies that Christ would call *Esau* within the corrupted nature of Adam, in the hatred

54. Therefore, this is the understanding of the Scripture: that the earthly *Adam*—living in his own will within the kingdom of *corrupt* nature—does not find, nor can he find, repentance. There is no ability for good within that nature; rather, the grace incorporated within *him* awakens or stirs up that ability when the will turns toward it. For if self-will could produce repentance and become good, honest, and virtuous on its own, *it would not need Grace*.

55. The decrees in Scripture point only to two kingdoms: namely <note>original: "viz."</note>, the "hardening" of hearts concerns the false and wicked will. The false will hardens itself; *God’s anger* within the will’s own substance *hardens it*. This hardening does not enter from the outside but is manifested within the will’s own substance. The will originates from God, and the *same* God introduces himself into the hardening within that will, in the same way that he introduces himself into hell in darkness and torment. The same should also be understood regarding the kingdom of Grace.

56. God wills in man *only* that which is good within the kingdom of his grace. Where the free will yields itself up to grace, there God wills what is good within that will *through Grace*.

57. But when someone says that a person cannot turn their will toward what is good—namely, toward grace—that claim is *groundless*. Indeed, grace stands in the abyss <note>The "abyss" (German: *Ungrund*) refers to the deep, hidden center of the soul where God's presence dwells.</note> of the creature in all wicked people, and the will only needs to "stand still" from its wicked works; then it begins, as its own self-will, to dive down into that abyss.

58. For that which stands still, stands still together with the Eternal One and becomes one *substance* with him, for it enters into its own "nothingness" <note>A mystical state of letting go of the ego and self-assertion.</note>. Must not the false will or desire—for the sake of a worldly law or for fear of punishment—refrain or "stand still" from unrighteous works? Why, then, can it not also do so for the sake of the *commandment* of God? If it can be obedient to a worldly lord and master and "stand still" for the purpose he requires, *why* not also for God? Especially when the *ability* is given as soon as a person merely inclines his will to stand still.

59. But the *reason* why the completely false, wicked will does not stand still and incline itself toward grace is because it is clearly born as a *thistle*, in which grace lies *too* deeply hidden, and the wrath of God is too strong in its nature. Grace draws it and shows it its own falsehood and wickedness; but the will *despises* <note>original: "contemneth"</note> grace and acts like a thistle <margin>† 2 Corinthians 2:15–16.</margin> does in the power of the sun. Such a one is to God † *a fragrance of death leading to damnation* in hell, so that grace may be separated from the false and wicked will.

60. However, the conclusions of human reason—which declare that God in himself (insofar as he is called God) has determined that *one portion of humanity*, and indeed the majority, shall and *must* be damned, and that he hardens them by his own *purposeful* will—are false. This has no basis either in the Scripture or in the light of nature, if a person only considers the Scripture rightly and does not look upon it blindly.

61. For in God, insofar as he is called God, there is no "purpose" nor any "beginning" to will; he is himself the will of the deep <note>original: "profundity"</note>—namely <note>original: "viz."</note>, the One alone,

## CHAPTER 64

### Concerning Esau's Genealogy: and the very excellent and emphatic allegory <note>original: "figure"</note> signified by Joseph, the son of Jacob; and what is to be understood by it.

#### Based on the 36th chapter of Genesis.

1. The thirty-sixth chapter of Genesis is the genealogy of the potent <margin>Genesis 36</margin> and princely family of Esau. It shows how God gave him much wealth, many children, and many grandchildren. The Spirit sets down a great register in describing his children and his children’s children, relating what great princes and dukes descended from him and possessed the glory of the world. Whereas, on the other side, when the Spirit speaks of Jacob, He does not mention any present worldly glory, but only speaks in the allegory of Christ concerning the kingdom to come.

2. By this, we see very clearly that Esau stands as a symbol <note>original: "figure"</note> of the kingdom of nature, and that the glory of nature fell to his lot. He became a great prince and fathered many princely families. We also see how God blessed him and made him great, and how the Holy Spirit, with special observation <margin>care and diligence</margin>, has recorded and specified his posterity. This signifies that we should learn to rightly understand the symbolism of Jacob and Esau, and not go on so blindly as to condemn Esau to the bottomless pit of hell, as is far too frequently done. For we see how his father, Isaac, did appoint and assign to him a very rich and wealthy habitation upon the earth, and that God would give him many temporal blessings. However, his symbol in Adam’s nature must perish, and Christ must arise in him, so that from ESAU the <margin>the swinish, bestial, earthy property</margin> "SAU" <note>In German, "Sau" means "sow" or "pig."</note> might be done away with, and he might remain steadfast in the <margin>the angelic, eternal property</margin> "E", as an Angel <note>original: "Sin Engel? / An Angel"</note>, which Christ in Jacob’s symbol would help him to become.

His soul was not yet defiled *from the outside* by the *art of lying*. The Spirit of God began to <margin>work, act, or move in him</margin> drive him forward, for his coat of many colors was a *symbol* <note>original: "figure"</note> of the inward.

37. This symbol prefigures and represents the image of a true young scholar and *beginner* in Christianity. It shows how one must be when the Spirit of God drives and acts upon them: namely, they must turn their *heart* to God, their Father, and learn to love Him sincerely. Just as *Joseph* loved to be with his father and told him of the evil committed among his children, so must a beginner in Christianity daily bring before God all their *own* miseries, as well as the miseries and *sins* of *all* who belong to them—indeed, of all *Christendom*. As *Daniel* confessed the sins of the people of *Israel* before God, and *Joseph* the evils of his brothers before his father, so a true Christian daily confesses the misery and *sin* of their people and nation with heartfelt compassion, praying that God would be *merciful* to them and preserve them from great evils and sins.

38. When this is achieved, their heart becomes very simple, honest, and *upright*. They desire *no* craftiness but would gladly have all things proceed righteously and justly. They cannot tolerate any unrighteousness or *devious dealings* <note>original: "suttle dealings"</note>, for they always confess the people's unrighteousness before God. Thus, their mind becomes altogether simple and seeks *no* kind of craftiness or subtlety. Instead, they put their hope and confidence in God and live in simplicity and *lowliness* of heart before God and the world. They are like the tender young lad, *Joseph*, for they hope for good continually from God, their Father.

39. Now, when a person has come this far, then *Joseph* [that is <note>original: "viz." (videlicet)</note>, the chaste, virginal child of *Sophia* <note>In the author's theology, "Sophia" refers to Divine Wisdom.</note>] is truly born. Then God, the Father, clothes their soul with the multicolored coat—namely, with *divine power*. Immediately, the Spirit of God within them begins to interact with the soul, just as He did with *Joseph*. For the Spirit of God sees through the soul and with the soul (just as *Joseph*, as a symbolic type, saw things that were to come represented to him in visions of dreams, through which the Spirit interacted with his soul). Even so, the Spirit of God immediately takes delightful communion with the soul of a new *Joseph*—that is, with the inward spiritual world.

20. In Judah lay the root of the Covenant, which pressed on to the Limit, where it should be manifested in Christ; and so Judah stood here in this figure in the place or stead of the divine Word. For he thought he was now at home, and went forth out of Paradise to eat earthly fruit, like the beasts or living creatures. Therefore the Spirit says here: *He sheared his sheep*; which might well be done by Judah, but the Spirit has here the most secret figure under which Adam is comprised. For the Spirit says: *Judah took his shepherd Hirah of Adullam along with him.*

For the same—namely <note>original: "viz."</note>, the earthly desire—was his shepherd. 31. Here the Spirit alludes very finely in the symbolic figure to how **Adam’s** Nature **lies** with the presented new **Eve** in the Covenant, and yet **knows her not**. It also shows how the Covenant lies with **Adam’s** first righteous Nature, and how they meet together in strange apparel. It wishes only to lie with the New **Eve** in its false, **seeming** holiness, and its heart is far from the true wedlock marriage. It only draws near her in a **hypocritical whoredom**, as is done in the Office of the Pharisees. Then this **Eve** says to the Adamic Nature, "What will you give me?" Both stood in the figure, showing how Christ should be manifested out of **Adam’s** nature in **Mary**, in whom lay and was manifested the right **Tamar**, or New **Eve**.

35. This is from the heavenly world’s substance, which faded or vanished in the Fall. 36. And just as *Tamar* did not ask for the kid, but wanted a significant pledge; so the Spirit of Christ in the Covenant does not ask for outward ceremony and pageantry where people offer gifts to it. It requires the body, soul, and spirit as a pledge.

37. In this symbolic figure, it represents the *Jewish* offerings as an act of prostitution <note>original: "whoredom"</note> in the *sight* of God. For just as *Judah* committed prostitution with *Tamar*—intending only the act and offering a kid for it—so also did the priests of the Law. In their appearance of holiness and hypocrisy, they played the harlot with God using the blood and flesh of *beasts*. This was indeed a symbol of the *inward* reality, and God was pleased to bear with it; however, he would not accept their offerings, nor did he join himself with the offering, but rather with the *faith* in the body, soul, and spirit of man, of which we have an excellent example.

38. *Judah* had fathered three sons by the *Canaanite* woman; but the line of the Covenant that resided in him would *not pass on* through the *Canaanite* woman and her children. Instead, it revealed itself through this sexual union <note>original: "whoredome"</note> of *Judah* with *Tamar*, resulting in *Perez*, whom *Tamar* conceived by *Judah* through this sexual act <note>original: "coition or lying together"</note>. With this symbol, God represents the misery of man and presents his Covenant of Grace through the *opening* of this precious line of the Covenant, which moved toward its *goal* <note>original: "limit"</note>, *Christ*. This occurred in the act of *Judah* and *Tamar*—that is <note>original: "viz."</note>, in the earthly *Adam* and the earthly *Eve*—but within the *inward* ground of its essence. This signifies that even the children of God in their corrupt nature do nothing but commit spiritual adultery in the presence of God, and that *their* state of marriage is but a defiled, animalistic <note>original: "beastiall"</note> thing in the presence of God, containing nothing chaste or *pure in the sight of God*. Therefore, the line of the Covenant revealed itself in this union of *Judah* and *Tamar* to show that Christ would come from this line of the Covenant and enter into the *middle* of this corruption as a Mediator. He would break the head of the false, lustful desire and the earthly serpent, and purify our impure, fleshly, animalistic conception with his heavenly virgin seed, and *in himself* transform it back into the paradisiacal image.

39. Also, God reveals the line of his Covenant in this act of *Judah* and *Tamar* so that his *wrath* toward our human impurity might not *burn up* and devour body and soul. Instead, the Covenant of Grace might withstand the anger directed at our impurity, lest God should devour *Israel* in their abominations and impurity in his wrath.

40. Now, seeing that the line of the Covenant—in terms of its manifestation and propagation—resided in *Judah*, and that *Israel* was also impure according to the nature of *Adam*, God represented his Covenant of Grace at its first propagation from the line of *Israel* in such a symbol. Thus, the faith of *Abraham*, *Isaac*, and *Jacob* in the *first* branch from them (namely <note>original: "viz."</note>, in *Judah* and his children) might withstand his wrath. In this way, the faith of *Abraham*—that is, the Spirit of Christ within *Abraham's* faith—might continually be a Mediator between God and the impurity of man.

59. O you wonderful, great God, who are so high and deep: how *simply*, and according to the capacity of a child, do you model your wisdom for us? What is all the art and wit of human *greatness* before you, who descend so very much, bow down, and *humble* yourself? You present your deepest wisdom and highest depth in a childish simplicity, which may justly *shame* all human status and self-made cleverness when they see such great mysteries of God expressed in such childishness.

60. O world, how foolish are you! You elevate yourself in a blind life and still cling to the *husk*, not seeing what you are and not understanding divine *simplicity*. How, then, will you perceive the divine depth? O, abandon your own cleverness and cling to simplicity, so that you may yet obtain a child’s understanding. Do not be accounted in the sight of God as *more unwise* than the beasts, which remain in their clothing and condition as God created them. O you world, why do you *sleep* in the Devil’s arms, who suckles and dandles you in himself, bringing you to his will and life by his power? O, do but see it!

61. This powerful figure in these twins—one of whom put out his hand, which the midwife bound with a red thread, thinking it would be the first, but it drew the hand back again and his brother came out—prefigures *this* for us: how Christ, in this line of the Covenant, assumed human nature. Thus, *human* nature, according to *Adam’s* right and self-will in this world, first puts itself forward and manifests itself. *Around which* Adamic nature, in the humanity of Christ, must this red thread—the shedding of his blood—be bound.

That is, *Adam’s* will, which had gone out, must again *return* into the mother’s womb—namely, be turned back into the Word—and then comes...

62. The inward "New Adam" comes forth, after which follows Adam’s nature with the red thread <note>original: "Thrid"; this refers to the scarlet thread tied to the hand of Zarah during birth in Genesis 38:28</note>. Then the Mother says to the New Adam in Christ, "Why have you made this breach for your will?" The Mother says "for your will," not for the sake of your will, but for the sake of that which drives your will forth. And Adam’s will goes back. Thus has the will in the Covenant of Grace powerfully broken through the strong bar and enclosure of the first principle—namely, the kingdom of God’s anger. For the good will in Adam was shut up in death and in hell; but in Christ, he tore that powerful rift and broke through death and hell back again into the kingdom of eternal nature. He turned himself forth again into the natural life, so that the kingdom of God was again manifested in human life.

63. The Spirit represents this through Tamar in the line of the Covenant and models Christ’s breakthrough through death and hell, showing how that should be. By this pre-modeling, the adulterous <note>original: "whorish"</note> will of Tamar and Judah was healed, and their children of adultery <note>original: "whoredome"</note> in the line of Christ were joined <note>original: "Espoused"</note> into the Covenant of Grace.

64. In Esau and Jacob stood the figure showing how, according to nature, Adam had the right of the kingdom and how he squandered it, and is therefore in his natural will thrust out from the kingdom of God, and how Christ came to help him. Here now stands the figure showing how Christ has obtained the kingdom and turned Adam back again, and in Adam turned himself forth, so that now Adam is called Christ. He presents himself very excellently in the figure of Joseph, and this stands fittingly and rightly in the interval of Joseph’s history.

65. For Joseph is the figure of a Christian; and this story of Judah and Tamar is a figure showing how a Christian springs out of Adam’s nature, and how Adam’s nature is turned in again and Christ turned forth. It shows how this image of a Christian man in this world is covered outwardly with the earthly Adam, so that men cannot recognize it. It also shows how Christ in Adam took his guilt upon him, and how Adam must be marked with this red thread, which mark is truly the pledge that Judah gave to Tamar. And I would have the reader advised in love not to reject our exposition of this text, but to consider it and look closely and clearly <note>original: "perspicuously"</note> into it; then he will well perceive who the expositor was, if he is worthy of it.

He is cast into the Pit—namely, *into Christ's suffering and death*—and then loses the Adamic inheritance of the kingdom of *this world*. When his will and mind are brought away from it, he must yield up his father’s house—that is, all his *selfhood* together with his *natural life*—to his brothers in his father’s house. This means he yields to the power of God in the *government* of this world and allows himself to be cast into the pit of the death of his natural will. In that pit, he gives himself up to the death of Christ and willingly dies to the will of this world (to his own Adamic house) and willingly *suffers* whatever his brothers of this world do to him.

8. Christ makes him living by his power and draws him, like *Joseph*, out of the pit and grave of death. He brings him into his service, just as *Joseph* entered the service of *Pharaoh's* Captain of the Guard. Then all goes prosperously in and with him, for the divine power rules him. *Now* he attains divine understanding and wisdom and knows how to manage his Master's goods; in the Christian figure <note>original: "figure"; here meaning a symbolic representation or type.</note>, that is as much as to say:

[The fallen human nature] made itself master of the governance within itself, and took the *essence* and things of this world as its own—as if the person had created it all and refused to be God’s servant in it. Such a person refuses to be a *guardian* and nourisher to their fellow branches <note>The author uses a vine metaphor where all humans are branches of the same life</note>, or to give them their strength, will, essence, and substance. Instead, they say, "It is mine; that is, it is my own. I will keep it *only for myself*, and it shall remain with me." God takes this selfish authority away from a Christian and instead makes them a guardian and nourisher of their brothers once again—namely, a steward for his Lord. He *lets them possess* the temporary goods they already had, provided they held them by natural right with righteousness and truth, and makes them like *Joseph* in that position.

10. This *Joseph* now *does not say*, "This is *mine*—that village, city, country, principality, kingdom, or empire." Nor does he say, "That house, land, field, money, those goods, that cattle, that woman, or that child is mine." Instead, he says with his whole heart and *conscience*, out of a new and good Christian will: "It *all* belongs to my *God* and His *children*. He has appointed me as a ruler, disposer, and *steward* of it. I must manage it for the purpose He intends. I should use it to sustain myself and His children, the needy, and I should be their curator <note>meaning a caretaker or guardian</note>. I should also give them my power, strength, and *understanding* of the divine gift, and instruct, tutor, or take care of them for their own good. Just as God governs me with His Spirit, so should I—as *His officer* in this world—use my understanding and office to govern my fellow members with *such* power..."

22. 23. Our Adamic nobility is lost in Adam, but whoever in this world in the Kingdom of Christ is noble, is noble in respect of their Office in which they serve. 24. This is also how we should understand the offices in this world.

25. 20. 24. Even so, God does awaken or manifest himself in his power in his "word of hearing," or divine sense, with man's pure humble voice or melody of praise.

25. For God has created angels and men for that purpose, namely for his own joy. ### CHAPTER 42. *Who appeared to Abraham.* Genesis 18. 297

In his humility, God then asked after *Sarah*, whom he well knew, but *Sarah* did not know him—not even that the Lord should appear in such a form. Then he said to *Abraham*, "*Where is your wife Sarah?*" This means she was not yet part of this Divine Play until she had received Abraham’s <term>Ens</term> <note>original: "Ens"; a Latin term used by the author to mean the essential being, inner essence, or spiritual substance of a thing.</note> of faith; and then this Play would awaken itself in her. Therefore she laughed at this, for she did not know the Mysteries; at that moment, they only manifested themselves in Abraham’s *spirit*, where the essence of faith lay. And he said, "*She is in the tent*"; that is:

27. She is in the human tent covered with the earthly tent, so that she does not see who is now with me. And the Lord said, "*I will come again to you, as I live <margin>German *So* signifies *As*, or *If*.</margin>, and behold! Sarah your wife shall have a son.*" That is: I will come again to you with the movement of your seed. And when *Sarah* shall conceive, then I will open and *release* her in her closed-up seed, and enter into your seed; that is, move. For "to come" signifies "to move": when God comes, he moves man, and comes or goes *within* and with man.

28. But when he says, "*As I live*," this is spoken in an essential manner; for God told him how he would come—not standing before him as he did at this time, but *as* <margin>Or, *If*.</margin> the light-filled *influence* and power of the sun gives itself into a fruit. When the sun comes, it does not merely step near the fruit, but it acts *as* a power: that is, it penetrates essentially into it. For "*as*" means "in this way: I will see into it [or open my love-aspect in the essence of its life]." "*As I live*"; here we are not to understand this as if he had said "if I am still living," but rather that he would live within that "as." He would come in the "as"—that is, essentially, and not figuratively or symbolically as he did at this time.

29. For when God comes, he comes in no other way than *as* the sunshine comes into the fruit. This is understood in the "language of nature" <note>Boehme's concept of the "language of nature" refers to a universal, spiritual language where the sound or form of a thing expresses its inner essence.</note> essentially, with emphatic excellence. For if God speaks of his own coming, then he speaks only essentially, in the nature and manner of the *uncompounded* language of the senses.

30. *And Sarah laughed at this*; she thought that she should bring forth a son from *Abraham’s* lust only, from human cohabitation in the carnal desire of the flesh. Therefore she said, "*Shall I, now that I and my lord are both old, take pleasure?*" The animalistic world-spirit laughed at its youth, seeing that it was now weak and should now again become youthful. It thought to itself that this was a joke: "As if you could!" It is as if one should tell an old man, "You shall become *young* again, and feel such desire and lust as when you were young." At this, nature would laugh and think, "Yes, indeed; if only that were true!" It was as if doubt and hope were coupled together. Thus it was also with *Sarah*, for the world-spirit does not understand the mysteries of God; before God, it is only like a beast. And because the world-spirit *now* heard that it should happen this way, it thought, "You shall be the master-worker; oh, if only you could, you would very gladly." And it laughed at itself for the idea that it should become young again.

31. The natural man understands as much about God as a beast does. When a beast sees hay, it thinks, "Now there is something for me to eat"; but if it sees nothing, then it hopes for it out of habit. But *Sarah* had now hoped until she was ninety years old, and thought it too...

3. It is true; reason wonders within itself whether this is so or not. Is He then limited <note>original: "circumscriptive"</note> <margin>Understandable or measurable.
