<meta>This page continues Jacob Boehme’s mystical interpretation of Genesis 43. Boehme explains how the physical journey of Jacob’s sons to Egypt represents the soul’s internal struggle to reach a state of true repentance and union with Christ (represented by Joseph). He focuses on why a second journey is necessary for the soul.</meta>

### Chapter 70. Jacob’s Sons went into Egypt again. Genesis 43. 525

17. And it also comes to pass that his conscience—though perhaps at first it is terrified—is in the end appeased, and divine food is given to him from the heavenly Joseph into the "sack" of his desire. Consequently, the anger of God lets him go. But the anger of God, in His righteousness, takes a <margin>Or, pawn.</margin> pledge from the conscience and keeps it to see whether the man will continue to remain satisfied with this burden of food. If not, then the anger of God retains its primary right over both soul and body.

18. This is what happens to us poor human beings: we very lightly and lavishly spend the first food that the heavenly Joseph gives us during our initial repentance. We then return to a state of great hunger, want, and misery of conscience, and we must become poor once again. This happens precisely because the first time, we did not bring along our Benjamin—namely <note>original: "viz."</note>, the most inward ground <note>In Boehme’s theology, the "inward ground" refers to the deepest, most essential part of the soul where God dwells.</note>. In that first attempt, our will was not quite broken; we merely supposed we would continue in repentance and divine resignation until our end. But if that surrender had been fully accomplished in the first repentance, then God’s righteousness in His anger could not have taken any pledge, but would have had to leave us entirely free.

19. This symbolic figure—that Jacob’s children had to go down into Egypt for food twice, and that Joseph was only revealed to them the second time, and that the third time they brought their wives, children, everything they owned, and their father—prefigures a spiritual truth. It shows that when a person, through sin, has spent and consumed the first divine food, he must hunger again and be in want in his conscience. His conscience presses him and complains, just as a hungry belly complains for food. Then he thinks back on his first repentance and how Grace was once bestowed upon him.

20. But his most inward ground—namely, the bond of God’s anger—complains against him and condemns him because he did not preserve that Grace. It blames him as an unfaithful, perjured man who tasted God’s Grace and saw how it was bestowed on him out of mere mercy <note>original: "meere Mercy"; meaning pure or absolute mercy.</note>, yet for the sake of fleshly lusts, he spoiled and lost it all again. Then he stands as one who is not worthy of anything—not even to look up to heaven or for the earth to bear him—because he squandered such a precious thing for base lusts. Yet, like the poor Publican and sinner, or the lost son <note>The Prodigal Son (Luke 15).</note> who kept the swine, he thinks he will turn back and come to the salvation of God. And then, for the first time, he is in "right true earnest." Then all of Jacob’s sons, one and all, go a second time into Egypt—into repentance—to buy heavenly grain. During this time, the Old Adamic Jacob—namely, the body—must stay at home in calamity.

21. It is in this state of earnestness that Benjamin—the inward ground—is finally brought along. Now the first will is broken; it no longer approaches with the same self-serving purpose as the first time. They no longer come as "spies" before Joseph, but as truly hungry men—that is, with a sincere, hungry life that hungers after God’s mercy and the food of Jesus Christ with all its powers and virtues.

22. Here now begins the earnestness in fear and trembling. This is the true journey toward heavenly food, where the conscience stands in anxiety and Reason despairs of its own ability, thinking: "Alas, God is angry with me; where shall I seek Grace?" I am...

<summary>Boehme interprets the second journey of Jacob's sons to Egypt as the "true earnest" stage of repentance, where the soul finally surrenders its "inward ground" (Benjamin) to God after failing to maintain its first experience of Grace.</summary>
